Introduction 1.1. Introduction of background This is a report of what we experienced as XDEZO's Laravel Developer Interns. We worked on the internship together on a real web application project where we were involved in both frontend and backend activities. We essentially set our sights on understanding how to create smooth, functional systems with Laravel- managing databases, handling user accounts, and bringing together various components of the application so that all the pieces talked to each other flawlessly. We also got to collaborate on online payment systems. This helped us learn how to use other services safely and efficiently. It made us realize not only the technical aspect, but also how to improve the system for users. In the process, we encountered setbacks such as debugging stubborn issues, learning to collaborate when under pressure, and trying to determine how to apply what we learned in class to real-life scenarios. This internship was a great experience for us to enhance our professional and technical capabilities. It made us more skilled in coding, boosted our confidence in developing real applications, and familiarized us with how software development teams work together in a company. In the below report, we have explained the work we did, the issues we faced, the methods we used, and the things we learned during our internship at XDEZO Technology. AHP 7 Hotel Booking System 1.2. Organization Profile XDezo Technology is a renowned IT company that offers state-of-the-art software and web solution which is located in Pokhara. Through its services such as custom software development, API integration, e-commerce platforms, and cloud-based systems, XDezo serves many industries while focusing on the delivery of high- performance, secure, and scalable solutions. XDezo ensures that its solutions are up-to-date and reliable by using modern tools such as React.js for dynamic user interfaces, and Laravel for backend development. With its commitment to best practices and constant innovation, the company has built a strong legacy as a dependable partner for businesses that want to improve their internet exposure and operational efficiency. AHP 8 Hotel Booking System 1.3. Introduction of the system The system we had developed during our internship is known as the Hotel Booking System – an online platform to make hotel bookings more convenient and convenient for customers and hotel admins. The primary objective of the system is to enable users to explore various hotel packages, verify details such as price, inclusions, and availability, and successively book the selected package online through secure payment options including eSewa. For the customer, the system offers a smooth and intuitive interface: they are able to register, log in, explore different packages, filter by price/package type, view photos and details, and book stress free on their device. On the admin side, the system also includes tools to manage packages, update availability, monitor bookings, and payments – it helps the hotel staff to take care of everything and keep it all in order. For the backend, we developed the system using Laravel, while the responsive frontend was created with the use of HTML, CSS, Bootstrap and JavaScript. We aimed at developing a dynamic, real time system where the data updates instantly, availability is always up to date and online payments are secure and verifiable. This project helped us in applying technical skills to a fully functioning product with solutions to actual user needs, synergically integrating system functionality with a good user experience. In the following sections of this report, we will talk about the system’s design, key features, development, and how all these deliver a functional hotel booking solution. AHP 9 Hotel Booking System 1.4. Aims and Objectives of system The main aim of the Hotel Booking system is to facilitate the smooth online platform where customers are easy to navigate hotel packages, get detailed inclusions, and do secure transactions through the integrated online payments, whilst hotel admins are given the tools to manage packages, bookings, and overtimes. • To develop a user-friendly web platform where customers can browse, filter, and book hotel packages online. • Creating a secure backend system using Laravel to handle users, packages, bookings, payments. • To incorporate the eSewa payment gateway for seamless and secure online transactions. • To create an Admin panel for the hotel staff to manage packages, track bookings and track payment status. • For updates on availability of packages in real time to minimize chances of double bookings or errors. AHP 10 Hotel Booking System 1.5. Functions of the system • User registration, login, and account administration. • Browsing and filtering of hotel packages with details. • Booking packages including real-time availability check. • Secure online payments using eSewa. • Admin panel to handle packages, bookings, and payments. AHP 11 Hotel Booking System 2. Planning and Analysis In this phase, we aimed at designing the system structure and flow. We designed the ERD to define data relationships, the DFD to map system processes, the Use Case Diagram to describe key user’s actions, and the User Flow to describe step-by-step interaction for both customers and admins. These tools provided us with a clear plan for the effective construction of the system. 2.1. Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD) Figure 1: Entity Relationship Diagram AHP 12 Hotel Booking System 2.2. Frontend Development The frontend development aimed at developing a user friendly, visually appealing interface through which users can easily navigate the hotel booking system. With the help of HTML, CSS, Bootstrap, and JavaScript, we developed responsive pages that flow well on desktop and mobile platforms. We stressed on the need for clear layouts, interactive features, and good speed when it came to creating a seamless and user- friendly experience. 3.1. Home Page • Created a header section that contains navigation links and a search bar for easy access to the available hotel packages. • Added a responsive hero image with hotel offers and promotions. • Designed an introduction page that showcases the top services and benefits of the hotel to interest users. • Developed a carousel for featured packages which shows popular packages with details such as price, duration and highlights. • Added a testimonial section that also contains previous customer testimonials, and footer with contact information, social media links, and policies. 3.2. Booking Functionality • Developed a booking form where individuals could choose packages, select dates, submit bookings, and find instructions straightforward. • Integrated real-time date validation for the purpose of ensuring package availability and preventing overbooking. • Added summary & confirmation steps so that users can review details before completing a booking. • Linked the booking process with the payment gateway for safe financial transfers. • Updated feedback messages to inform the customers on successful bookings or input errors. AHP 17 Hotel Booking System 3.3. Contact us Page • Created a contact form to collect user name, email, subject, and message for inquiries/feedback. • Implemented validation checks to verify information submitted by users is complete and accurate. • Shown hotel contact information such as phone number, email address, and its location. • Added an embed for Google Map to provide ready reference for the location. • Made sure the form sends messages securely and confirms a success. 3.4. Package Page • Developed a listing page that lists all the available hotel packages with the prices, durations, and brief descriptions. • Provide dynamic filter options (e.g., price range, type of package) in order to allow users to narrow down their search. • Automated package sorting by popularity, price, or newest. • Integrated “View Details” buttons with links to the details page of the full package. • Package availability status and booking options were clearly shown. 3.5. Room Page • Constructed a detailed room page containing pictures, descriptions, and included facilities for each package. • Highlighted room types (single, double, suite) and occupancy permits. • Additional pricing information and any special deals tied to room bookings. • Provided a gallery or slideshow option for users to review room visuals. • Clear booking buttons and availability indicators for every room type. AHP 18 Hotel Booking System 4. Backend Development Backend Development was an essential part of the Hotel Booking System, and we developed a secure and smooth-working system using Laravel. We set up the project, prepared the database, developed models, controllers, and migrations for main parts such as users, packages, rooms, booking, payments, events, and contact messages. We also integrated the system with eSewa so users could make online payments securely for bookings and events. In order to ensure everything was working smoothly, we added checks and error handling so that bookings and payments only got confirmed upon successful transactions and user messages were processed by their intended destinations. We also established Laravel routes that would enable the frontend to be connected to the backend, ensuring seamless integration between all the functioning parts of the system. These routes managed user orders such as browsing packages, booking rooms, paying payments, and sending contact messages, and admin operations, for example managing packages, rooms, bookings, and events. Each route was properly connected to the appropriate controller and method, which kept it neatly organized, secure, and maintainable. 4.1. Set up for Laravel The first step in building the backend was to configure the Laravel, set the environment, and connect the project to the MySQL database. We have made database migrations for the core tables that involve users, packages, rooms, events, bookings, payments, and messages. We created user and admin access through the use of authentication, middleware, and route groups, which provided a strong foundation to develop the entire backend. AHP 19 Hotel Booking System 4.2. CRUD Functionality (Packages, Events, Rooms) We had complete CRUD (Create, Read, Update, and Delete) functionalities for the management of the hotel packages and events and the room data. Administrators can easily create new records, examine and alter particulars, or delete outdated info, all made easier by the Laravel’s models, controllers, and views. 4.3. Redirect Handling (Payments, Bookings, Contact Us) Backend logic was created to guide users appropriately after critical events, such as payment completion, booking submission, and sending messages. These redirects lead to confirmation or success pages, ensuring that a seamless and user-friendly experience is provided in the system. 4.4. eSewa Payment Integration The eSewa payment was added to guarantee that users can make safe and rapid online transactions. This feature enables users to process payments for bookings and events directly through the platform, and automated backend does not confirm bookings until the payment is confirmed. 4.5. Booking Management The backend handles the booking process from end to end, including saving user choices, dates, maintaining inventory, and checking reservations. We also introduced the backend validation system to protect from multiple bookings and ensure all booking records are properly stored in the database. 4.6. Contact Message Processing We developed a backend infrastructure to administer and store communications received via users’ contact forms. The contact form messages are safely saved into the database therefore giving the admins the opportunity to be able to respond to user inquiries in a timely manner. AHP 20 Hotel Booking System 4.7. Route Management We organized Laravel routes so that the frontend and backend could effortlessly synchronize. User routes handle things like browsing, booking, filling out contact forms, and paying, whereas admin routes deal with creating, reading, updating, and deleting packages, events, and rooms. We handled the organization, security, and user access of the system by employing the right controller links, route grouping and middleware. AHP 21 Hotel Booking System 5. Challenges and Solution During the development of the hotel booking system, we faced a number of major challenges. We made sure that we read the eSewa’s API documentation very carefully when we were configuring payment gateway and we added a server side validation to ensure that bookings were confirmed only after payment was processed. Working with real-time availability was an issue, we resolved it using backend validation in order to prevent conflicts and double bookings. We put a lot of effort into developing a smooth user flow from a booking stage to the payment and confirmation, outlining each action and updating both frontend and routes correspondingly. We also implemented Laravel middleware and route groups to manage security for admins and users to organize and validate their authorized areas. Finally, in order to ensure the frontend got the latest and reactive information about packages, rooms, and events, we developed optimized backend searches. AHP 22 Hotel Booking System 6. Outcomes and Deliverables When we completed the project, we had delivered a fully functional hotel book platform that caters to both the user and admin facilities. Users can register and log in to the system, browse hotel packages, view specific room details, reserve accommodations or events, and make payments securely using eSewa. Administrators are provided with a separate backend interface to monitor packages, rooms, events, bookings, payment transactions, and quickly resolve users’ concerns. Our project guaranteed success of crucial components, such as the Laravel backend which is managed in accordance with MVC principles, an organized MySQL database, and a dynamic frontend with the use of HTML, CSS, Bootstrap, and JavaScript to ensure a consistent user experience across all platforms. To make it more usable, we added interactive functions such as search bars, booking forms, dynamic filters, and carousels. Apart from establishing the technical infrastructure, the project offered substantial practical learning. Through practical application of the theoretical lessons, we consolidated our full-stack development skills while working on this project. We gained first-hand experience on backend coding, database modelling, development of user- friendly interfaces and integration of the external systems notable was the experience of working with eSewa payment service. We also developed our teamwork, communication, and problem-solving skills by working side-by-side, overseeing common duties, meeting deadlines, and collectively solving technical problems. Not only did this project provide an operational hotel booking system, but it also gave personal and professional development. AHP 23 Hotel Booking System 6.1. Version Control and GitHub Collaboration Throughout the course of the project, it is worth noting that Git and GitHub were instrumental in the organization and streamlining of our team’s efforts in development. In order for them to collaborate seamlessly, we established a common GitHub repository for updates, which would ensure the respective team members stayed in the loop with regards to the changes and have an organized development cycle. We capitalized on branches to separate project milestones like feature improvement from day-to-day development to ensure there is less interference in the main codebase. Our team followed some important version control practices, such as writing descriptive commit notes, being cautious with pull requests, code review, and prompt resolution of merge conflicts. Through following these practices, we were able to ensure that we always had consistent and high-quality code, as well as promote better collaboration and problem-solving skills among the team members. Being exposed to Git and GitHub for the entirety of the project stretched our understanding of professional version control methods which will benefit us significantly moving forward in terms of working in the real world software development scenarios. 2. Planning and Analysis

2.1 ERD (Entity Relationship Diagram)

The Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD) is a crucial part of our system design, as it visually represents how different entities in the database are related to each other. For SmartDocs, we identified the core entities as User, Editor, Admin, Category, Document, Article, Report, Feedback, and Comment. These entities are interlinked through relationships that ensure smooth data flow and logical storage. For example, a user can create multiple feedback entries, while each feedback is linked to one specific user. Similarly, articles and reports belong to a particular category, ensuring structured classification.

The ERD also ensures data normalization, preventing redundancy and maintaining consistency across the database. For instance, instead of storing user details repeatedly in each article or report, we only store a reference (foreign key) to the user entity. This approach minimizes storage inefficiency and allows easy updates when user details change. The relationships defined in the ERD also ensure data integrity, as foreign keys restrict invalid references and keep the database consistent.

By creating this ERD, we were able to visualize the backend structure of SmartDocs before implementing it in Laravel using Eloquent ORM. The diagram gave us clarity about how to design migrations and define relationships such as hasMany, belongsTo, and belongsToMany. It acted as a roadmap that reduced confusion during implementation and ensured a reliable, scalable database design.

2.2 DFD (Data Flow Diagram)

The Data Flow Diagram (DFD) provided a clear understanding of how data moves within SmartDocs. It depicts the interaction between external entities (users, editors, and admins) and the internal processes of the system. At the context level (Level 0 DFD), we represented SmartDocs as a single process, showing users interacting with it for actions like login, registration, feedback submission, and article/document access.

Moving further, the Level 1 and Level 2 DFDs break the system into detailed processes, such as “User Registration,” “Article Management,” “Category Handling,” and “Feedback Processing.” For instance, when a user submits feedback, the data flows from the user to the feedback process, which then interacts with the database and finally returns confirmation. Similarly, when an editor uploads a document, the process ensures validation, storage, and linking with the right category.

The DFD was useful not just for system planning but also for communication with our mentors and teammates. It helped everyone visualize the logical flow of information without requiring deep technical knowledge. This ensured alignment among all team members, minimized miscommunication, and created a shared understanding of how the system works internally.

The Use Case Diagram highlights the interaction between users and the system by outlining their possible actions. For SmartDocs, the three primary actors are Admin, Editor, and User. Editors can create, edit, and delete articles or reports, while Users can register, explore content, like/comment, and download documents.

By mapping these use cases, we ensured that the requirements of each actor were captured systematically. It provided a visual reference for the functionalities needed, which later guided our development roadmap. The diagram also helped us identify overlaps between roles, such as both Editors and Admins having the authority to manage content but with different levels of access.

The importance of this diagram lies in bridging the gap between technical and non-technical perspectives. It provided a high-level view of how the system is expected to behave without delving into the internal processes. This clarity was especially useful during team discussions and requirement validation with mentors.

This visualization also played a key role in frontend UI/UX design, ensuring that every feature was placed logically according to user expectations. By aligning the system’s navigation with user flows, we were able to make SmartDocs more intuitive, user-friendly, and efficient for all types of users.

3. System Design

3.1 System Architecture

The architecture of SmartDocs follows the MVC (Model-View-Controller) design pattern provided by Laravel. This ensures a clear separation of concerns, where Models handle the database logic, Views manage the frontend presentation, and Controllers control the application logic and communication between components. This structure made the system more maintainable, scalable, and easier to test during development.

In this architecture, the Model represents entities such as User, Article, Document, Report, Category, and Feedback. Each model interacts with the database using Laravel’s Eloquent ORM, ensuring relationships like one-to-many and many-to-many are properly maintained. The Controller acts as the middle layer, processing requests from the frontend and returning the appropriate response. For example, when a user requests to download a document, the controller validates permissions, fetches the file, and returns it to the user. The View is built using Blade templates, providing a clean and reusable structure for the user interface.

This layered design helped us build SmartDocs with flexibility. Future modifications such as adding new roles, introducing premium features, or extending analytics will be easier because of the modular architecture. It also enhances security and performance, as each layer has a specific responsibility, reducing the risk of errors and vulnerabilities.

3.2 Database Design

The database design of SmartDocs is based on the ERD we created earlier. It consists of multiple relational tables including users, editors, admins, categories, articles, documents, reports, feedbacks, and comments. Each table is structured with primary keys, foreign keys, and constraints to ensure data consistency. For example, the articles table contains a foreign key category_id linking it to the categories table, while user_id links the article to its creator.

Normalization played a key role in our database design. Instead of duplicating data, we ensured that related information was stored in separate tables. For instance, user details are stored only once in the users table, while references are made through IDs in other tables such as feedbacks or documents. This prevents redundancy, reduces storage inefficiency, and ensures accuracy whenever updates occur.

We also designed the database with scalability and performance in mind. Indexing was applied on frequently queried fields like category_id and user_id, ensuring faster searches and retrievals. This makes the system capable of handling large volumes of documents and users without slowing down. The structured database design guarantees data integrity, security, and reliability for SmartDocs.

3.3 User Interface (UI) Design

The User Interface (UI) of SmartDocs was designed with a modern and minimalistic approach. We focused on keeping the layout clean, ensuring users could easily navigate between sections such as documents, articles, categories, and reports. The dashboard was designed separately for each role (Admin, Editor, and User) with customized features according to their responsibilities. For example, Admin dashboards emphasize statistics and management, while User dashboards focus on browsing and interacting with content.

We implemented Blade templating to create reusable UI components, such as navigation bars, footers, and side menus. This not only ensured consistency across all pages but also reduced repetitive coding. Tailwind CSS was integrated to provide a responsive design that adapts seamlessly across devices, ensuring accessibility for desktop, tablet, and mobile users. This responsiveness was crucial since users might access SmartDocs from different environments.

Special attention was given to user experience (UX) by aligning the interface with the user flows we planned earlier. Buttons, dropdowns, and forms were strategically placed for quick actions. For example, editors can upload an article in just two steps, and users can submit feedback with minimal clicks. The UI was tested with different color schemes, and we finalized a professional yet simple palette that enhances readability and user engagement.

3.4 Security Design

Security was a top priority in designing SmartDocs. We implemented role-based access control (RBAC) to ensure that users, editors, and admins can only access features relevant to their role. For example, a normal user cannot delete or edit an article, while admins have the highest level of privileges to manage the entire system. This was enforced both at the controller level and middleware level to prevent unauthorized access.

Authentication and authorization were handled using Laravel Breeze, which provided secure login and registration features. Passwords were encrypted using hashing (bcrypt), ensuring sensitive information is not stored in plain text. Additionally, measures such as CSRF protection, input validation, and SQL injection prevention were included to safeguard against common web vulnerabilities.

To further enhance data security, we implemented file protection for documents and reports, ensuring only authorized users could download them. Logging and auditing features were also planned, allowing admins to monitor suspicious activities within the system. This comprehensive security design makes SmartDocs a trustworthy platform for managing knowledge and documents.

4. System Implementation

4.1 Development Environment Setup

The implementation of SmartDocs began with setting up the development environment. Since the project was built using Laravel Breeze, the environment required PHP, Composer, MySQL, and Node.js to be properly configured. The project folder was placed inside the htdocs directory of XAMPP for local hosting, making it easy to run and test on localhost. Git was also integrated to maintain version control, allowing smooth collaboration and tracking of changes.

Laravel Breeze was installed to handle authentication scaffolding, providing secure login, registration, and password management features out of the box. This saved significant development time while ensuring best practices for security. The installation also included Tailwind CSS for styling and Alpine.js for lightweight frontend interactivity. These tools ensured that the project followed a modern stack with a balance of functionality and simplicity.

During the setup phase, environment variables were configured in the .env file, such as database connections, mail services, and application keys. This separation of configuration from code enhanced flexibility and security. Once the environment was stable, we moved to the development of system modules, starting with authentication, user management, and then gradually implementing documents, articles, reports, and feedback features.

4.2 Backend Implementation

The backend was developed using Laravel’s MVC architecture, which allowed clean separation between logic, database handling, and presentation. Controllers were created for different modules such as ArticleController, DocumentController, ReportController, and FeedbackController. Each controller was responsible for handling requests, applying business logic, and returning responses to the frontend.

Eloquent ORM was extensively used for database interaction. For example, the User model defined relationships with articles, documents, and feedbacks, while the Category model was linked to multiple articles and documents. These relationships enabled us to fetch data using simple, readable syntax such as $user->articles instead of writing complex SQL queries. This not only improved code readability but also reduced the chances of errors.

Additional backend features included middleware for role-based access control, ensuring only authorized roles could access specific routes. Validation was also applied in controllers before saving or updating records, preventing invalid or harmful data from entering the database. Together, these backend implementations ensured a strong, secure, and reliable system foundation.

4.3 Frontend Implementation

The frontend was implemented using Blade templates and Tailwind CSS, ensuring a consistent design across all pages. Reusable components such as headers, navigation menus, and footers were placed in layouts to avoid duplication and maintain a uniform look. Each page for users, editors, and admins was designed separately while reusing as many components as possible.

JavaScript was added to improve interactivity, such as confirmation popups for delete actions, search filtering, and category-based content loading. For example, on the documents.blade.php page, editors could filter documents by date or category without refreshing the page. Similarly, modals were used for editing articles and confirming user actions, making the interface smoother and more user-friendly.

The frontend design prioritized simplicity and usability. We ensured that the most important actions, such as uploading a document, giving feedback, or viewing reports, were accessible within just a few clicks. The responsive design, powered by Tailwind, allowed the application to adapt to different screen sizes, providing a consistent experience on desktops, tablets, and mobile devices.

4.4 Authentication & Role Management

Authentication and role management were key parts of implementation. Laravel Breeze provided the base authentication system, including login, registration, email verification, and password reset. On top of this, we added custom role-based access control (RBAC) for three main roles: Admin, Editor, and User.

Roles were stored in the users table with a role column. Middleware was written to check roles before accessing certain routes. For example, if a normal user attempted to access an editor-only page, the middleware would block the request and redirect them to an error or home page. This ensured that sensitive operations like approving articles or deleting documents were restricted to authorized users only.

We also extended role-based features to the UI. For instance, Admin dashboards displayed system statistics, Editor dashboards provided content management tools, and User dashboards focused on browsing and interacting with documents. This gave each role a tailored experience while maintaining centralized authentication.

4.5 Testing & Debugging

Testing was an ongoing process throughout implementation. We applied both manual and automated testing to ensure system stability. Manual testing was done by simulating different user roles and performing actions like uploading, editing, and deleting documents. This helped us confirm that permissions and workflows were functioning as intended.

For automated testing, Laravel’s built-in testing tools were used. Unit tests were written for controllers and models to validate key functionalities. For example, we tested whether users could only access documents they had permission for and whether editors could successfully update articles. These tests helped catch issues early and improved system reliability.

Debugging was made easier using Laravel’s error handling system. Error logs were tracked in storage/logs, which helped us identify and fix database query issues, missing views, or validation errors. By the end of testing, the system was stable, secure, and ready for deployment.

5. Testing & Evaluation

Testing was an essential phase of the SmartDocs development process to ensure the system functioned as intended, provided a smooth user experience, and performed well under different conditions. Different forms of testing were conducted, including functional testing, usability testing, and performance testing. Each stage helped identify issues and refine the system before final deployment.

5.1 Functional Testing
Functional testing focused on verifying whether each module worked according to the defined requirements. Features such as user registration, login, CRUD operations for articles and documents, role-based access (Admin, Editor, User), and feedback submission were tested thoroughly. Test cases were executed for both valid and invalid inputs to ensure proper validation, redirection, and error handling. For example, if a user attempted to register with an already used email, the system displayed an appropriate error message. Similarly, article creation, editing, and deletion were tested to confirm accurate database operations.

5.2 Usability Testing
Usability testing was performed to evaluate the interface design and navigation flow. The focus was on ensuring that users (admin, editors, and normal users) could easily interact with the system without confusion. Elements such as the dashboard layout, categories page, and top performer section were tested for clarity and accessibility. Feedback from peers and supervisors suggested improvements in button placement, form validation messages, and consistency in the light/dark mode theme. These refinements improved overall user experience, making the system intuitive and user-friendly.

5.3 Performance Testing
Performance testing was conducted to assess how well the system responded under different loads. The focus was on page load speed, database query efficiency, and responsiveness across multiple devices. By optimizing queries and reducing redundant database calls, system performance was enhanced. Tests were run for scenarios such as multiple users logging in simultaneously or several editors uploading documents at once. The system maintained stable performance with minimal lag, proving it reliable for real-world usage.

5.4 Results & Evaluation
The overall testing results confirmed that the SmartDocs system successfully met the defined objectives. Functional modules operated as expected, usability testing validated the system’s simplicity, and performance evaluation demonstrated stable operation. Minor issues, such as error message alignment and inconsistent color schemes, were identified and resolved. The final outcome was a functional, user-friendly, and performance-optimized system, ready for deployment and further scaling in professional environments.

5. Testing & Evaluation

Testing was one of the most crucial stages in the development of the Documentation Management System, as it ensured that the system performed according to the requirements and delivered a reliable experience for all users. We began with functional testing, where we carefully verified the behavior of each feature against the expected outcomes. User registration, login, and authentication were tested using both valid and invalid credentials to confirm that only authorized access was granted. Similarly, CRUD operations for articles, categories, and documents were tested to ensure accuracy in database transactions. Role-based access control was another important focus area—admins, editors, and normal users were each tested under different scenarios to confirm that they had the correct permissions, with admins enjoying full control, editors being limited to content management, and users restricted to read-only access. These functional checks guaranteed that every module worked as intended and followed the project’s specifications.

Alongside functional testing, usability testing was carried out to evaluate how intuitive and user-friendly the system was for different roles. Since the platform was designed for both technical and non-technical users, it was important that navigation remained simple and consistent. We tested the clarity of the dashboard, category browsing, search functionality, and article detail pages to ensure smooth interactions. Initial feedback highlighted areas such as button placement, message consistency, and the alignment of forms. After refining these elements, the interface became much more responsive and visually coherent. Additionally, accessibility across different devices and screen sizes was checked to confirm that the system could be used comfortably on desktops, laptops, and mobile devices. This stage ensured that users could quickly learn and adapt to the system without confusion or the need for additional training.

Lastly, performance testing was conducted to determine how the system behaved under various loads and conditions. We simulated multiple users accessing the system simultaneously to analyze speed, database response times, and system stability. Page load times were monitored and optimized by minimizing redundant database queries and applying caching where necessary. During these tests, the system was able to handle multiple concurrent logins, document uploads, and article browsing activities without significant delays or crashes. Although some minor inconsistencies, such as slower responses when handling large file uploads, were observed, these were resolved through optimization. In the end, the evaluation showed that the Documentation Management System was not only functionally sound and user-friendly but also stable and efficient, making it well-suited for real-world deployment in an organizational setting.
